074:1: Why did Adam and Eve, arriving in an isolated world, refuse worship and point only to the Father?
074:4: In Paper 73 we saw how Van and Amadon and the descendants of the Nodites prepared the Garden of Eden to receive Adam and Eve. Adam and Eve arrived on Urantia 37,848 years before A.D. 1934, in the season when the Garden was in full bloom (74:0.1).
074:5: Their bodies were rematerialized over ten days in the precincts of the Father's temple, and the two regained consciousness at the same moment. 074:6: In a world isolated by rebellion, then, what did these two beings teach first, and what path did they choose before people who wanted to raise them up as gods?

Twenty thousand years ago the ancestors of the Chinese established a dozen centers of primitive culture and learning along the Yellow River and the Yangtze, and mixed peoples coming from Sinkiang and Tibet strengthened them (79:6.5). The book names four factors that allowed the ancient yellow men to forge ahead (79:6.6).
079:62: Little mixture; later received red, Andonite, and Andite strains
079:64: Peace among their own kind; the first racial solidarity and large-scale civilization
079:66: Worship of the One Truth proclaimed by Singlangton

079:70: From 25,000 to 5000 B.C. the highest large-scale civilization on Urantia was in central and northern China (79:6.8). Above all, a religion that enshrined truth as the supreme Deity spurred them to explore the laws of nature and the potentials of human beings. That is why China forged ahead while India languished (79:6.10-6.11).
079:72: The stimulus of a progressive and advanced religion is often a decisive factor in cultural development. (79:6.10)
079:75: About fifteen thousand years ago the Andites crossed the Ti Tao pass, entered the upper Yellow River valley, and advanced as far as Honan (79:7.1). They were few in number, yet within a few thousand years the Yellow River settlements had pulled ahead of the Yangtze villages. The text says the reason was not superior numbers or culture, but that the blending produced a more versatile people. A moderate infusion stimulated their native minds without upsetting their inherent stability (79:7.2-7.3).
079:76: The Andites brought the traditions of Eden and Dalamatia, so early Chinese legends placed the land of the gods in the west (79:7.4). After 10,000 B.C. the Chinese built cities and began manufacturing, and all the arts of metalworking and manufacture date from this time (79:7.5). The similarities between the calendars, astronomy, and ways of government of China and Mesopotamia are due to exchanges by traders traveling through Turkestan (79:7.6).
079:78: Once the conquest of eastern Asia was complete, China lost the stimulus of outside threats and gradually became a peaceful agricultural people (79:8.1-8.2). An awareness of the past, the conservatism of an agricultural population, and a well-developed family life gave rise to ancestor veneration (79:8.3). The longing to seek new and higher truth was overshadowed by a tendency to venerate what was already established, and the civilization that had been advancing most rapidly came to a standstill (79:8.4).
079:83: A backward-looking philosophy that treats the past as the only source of truth
079:85: Gave the family the highest value, producing cultural stability and continuity

079:90: Filial piety and loyalty to the family created enduring family groups, and these fostered four factors that safeguard civilization (79:8.10).

079:101: A strong sense of duty, and growth in morality and ethical sensitivity
079:103: Over almost forty thousand years, despite many setbacks, Chinese civilization comes closest of all to a picture of unbroken progress. The text says that the white races have never surpassed the Chinese in family loyalty, group ethics, or personal morality (79:8.16). This civilization, which long dwelt on the glories of its past, is now awakening again as it looks afresh toward the transcendent goals of mortal existence (79:8.17).
079:105: Paper 79 shows what the Andites left to India and China as they flowed eastward. In India they left Dravidian civilization and the seeds of monotheism, but amid a land shut in by the sea, the tide of absorption, and a religion that lost its way, the early promise was not fulfilled. In China, peace among their own kind and the worship of the One Truth produced the highest large-scale civilization, but when the zeal for new truth turned into veneration of the past, that civilization stood still. Together the two stories teach a clear lesson: bloodlines and institutions alone cannot preserve a civilization, and true religion that reaches toward living truth is the higher energy that drives civilization forward. And both civilizations are waiting for the day when they will awaken again.

079:112: Geography and absorption postponed the promise of India
079:114: The Dravidians built a versatile city civilization
079:116: Not caste but true religion carries civilization forward
079:118: The yellow man, who learned peace and unity, took over eastern Asia

080:1: How did Adam's descendants, flowing out of Mesopotamia, become the foundation of European and Mediterranean civilization?
080:4: In Paper 79 we saw the Andites spread into the Orient: Turkestan, India, and China. Now Paper 80 turns westward. The book explains that the blue man of Europe did not by himself achieve a great civilization, but when he combined with the Adamized strains and with the Andites who came after them, he became one of the most powerful stocks for producing an aggressive civilization (80:0.1).
080:5: According to the book, the modern white peoples carry the Adamic stock blended with the Sangik races, especially the blue, and they also hold a good deal of the original Andonic strain and of the early Nodite blood (80:0.2). This paper follows in turn how changes in climate and land, the coming of the horse, and migrations along islands and rivers shaped the races and cultures of the West.
080:6: By what roads, then, did the wave of culture that began in Eden reach Europe, Egypt, and Greece, and what was gained and what was lost along the way?
080:8: ⟦Q 80:9.15⟧But it is a fallacy to presume to classify the white peoples as Nordic, Alpine, and Mediterranean.⟦/Q⟧ (80:9.15)
080:12: Even before the last Andites were driven out of the Euphrates valley, many of their kin had entered Europe as adventurers, teachers, traders, and warriors. At that time the Gibraltar isthmus and the Sicilian land bridge closed off the Mediterranean basin, and on those inland lakes mankind's earliest maritime trade took place (80:1.1). The Nodites built a widespread culture in the eastern Mediterranean, and the Syrians brought pottery, agriculture, domesticated animals, and metalworking to the Nile delta (80:1.2-1.3).
080:13: The book explains that the Adamites chose to unite with the blue men of Europe rather than with the distant red and yellow men. The blue men had none of the religious practices the Adamites disliked, and there was a strong attraction between the two races (80:1.5-1.6). The book records that in the course of this union the remnants of the Neanderthal strains were exterminated and blue groups such as the Cro-Magnons were formed (80:1.7). For these reasons the early waves of Mesopotamian culture flowed almost entirely into Europe (80:1.8).
080:15: ⟦Q 80:1.8⟧And it was these circumstances that determined the antecedents of modern European civilization.⟦/Q⟧ (80:1.8)
080:18: As the northern ice sheets retreated, the rain-bearing winds shifted northward, and the grasslands of the Sahara gradually turned to desert. This drought scattered the inhabitants of the Saharan highlands (80:2.1-2.2). The book says that this secondary Sangik substratum suggests a kinship among modern peoples spread from the Deccan to both shores of the Mediterranean (80:2.3).
080:23: South — to the forests of central Africa
080:25: Spain and adjacent Europe — the nucleus of the Mediterranean race
080:27: Arabia, northern Mesopotamia, India, and Ceylon
080:31: About the same time Britain was cut off from the continent and Denmark rose from the sea. When the Gibraltar isthmus collapsed in an earthquake and the Sicilian land bridge sank, the Mediterranean became one sea joined to the Atlantic, and this cataclysm brought the greatest loss of life by flood in human history (80:2.4). With the western route closed, the Adamites pushed north and east, entered Europe from the east by way of Turkestan, and found that the culture of the blue men there lagged thousands of years behind that of Asia (80:2.5).
080:33: The cultural centers of the blue man lay along the rivers of Europe, and thirty-five thousand years ago they were already a people of many mixed strains (80:3.1-3.2). The early European civilization after Adam was a fusion of the vigor and art of the blue man with the creative imagination of the Adamites, but the book explains that the blue man greatly lowered the cultural and spiritual level of the Adamites, so that European religion stayed at a low level for ten thousand years (80:3.3). On the other hand, the blue men were honest in all their dealings and respected chastity (80:3.4).
080:38: Efficient training of children, taught by both parents
080:40: Hunting, fishing, and gathering; boatbuilding; log huts and caves
080:42: Brave and farsighted, honest in dealings
080:44: Reached its peak about fifteen thousand years ago
080:46: About fifteen thousand years ago, as the Alpine forests spread widely, the people of Europe changed from hunters into herders, fishermen, and farmers (80:3.8). The book explains that this change brought biologic regression along with cultural progress. In settled life captives were kept as slaves, and this trend continued until the last great Mesopotamian invasions launched the civilization of the white race (80:3.9).
080:48: The Andites entered Europe in seven major invasions, and the last migrants came on horseback in three great waves. The earlier, purer strains passed through the steppes of the Volga and Don rivers to northwestern Europe (80:4.1). The Adamites were peaceful and the Nodites warlike; as the two lines mixed, and then mixed again with the Sangik races, they became the aggressive Andites who actually carried out military conquest (80:4.3).
080:49: The book says that the horse was the factor that settled Andite dominance in the West. The slow earlier waves scattered the farther they went from Mesopotamia, but the swift cavalry waves reached Europe as cohesive groups that kept their high culture (80:4.4). The book explains that as they passed over the Russian plains they fused with the blue men and became the ancestors of the so-called Nordic race—the Scandinavians, Germans, and Anglo-Saxons (80:4.5-4.6).
080:51: For three thousand years the military headquarters of the northern Andites was in Denmark, and as the waves of conquest spread out from there, the share of Andite blood grew smaller and the share of white grew larger (80:5.2). The decisive struggle between the blue men and the whites took place in the valley of the Somme, and the Cro-Magnons held out for more than five hundred years before giving way. Thor, who led this struggle, became a hero of the northern tribes and was later worshiped by some as a god (80:5.4).
080:52: The book records that later conquest proceeded by commercial penetration, population pressure, intermarriage, and the removal of those who were not assimilated, so that the blue men quickly disappeared (80:5.5-5.6). The blue strain gave the white Europeans their sturdiness and physical vigor, and the Andites gave them humor and imagination. The book says this union caused a cultural lag for a time, but its latent abilities finally showed themselves in today's European civilization (80:5.7-5.8).
080:62: As the culture of the Euphrates valley declined, the center of civilization moved to the Nile valley. Egypt succeeded Mesopotamia as the headquarters of the most advanced group on earth (80:6.1). By about 5000 B.C. Egypt held seven distinct human groups, all but one of which had come from Mesopotamia (80:6.2). Andite artisans, at home with rivers, floods, and irrigation, greatly advanced metalworking in the sheltered setting of the Nile (80:6.3).
080:63: The Egyptians gathered their city gods into a system of national gods and kept a vast priesthood. An attempt to revive the teachings of the Sethites did not last long. Egypt's first stone pyramid was built by Imhotep, an architect of Andite origin, but afterward the art of building declined, and through civil war and the inflow of outside tribes social progress slipped backward for more than five hundred years (80:6.4-6.5).
080:65: While Mesopotamian culture was waning, a superior civilization flourished for a time on the islands of the eastern Mediterranean (80:7.1). Around 12,000 B.C. an Andite tribe moved to Crete, and about two thousand years later descendants of Adamson, led by Sato, entered Greece (80:7.2-7.3). The book explains that the art and genius of the Greeks were an inheritance from the descendants of Adamson and his second wife, of Nodite descent, and that this is why the Greeks had myths of descent from the gods (80:7.5).
080:70: About 12,000 B.C.; small in build; skilled in textiles, metals, pottery, plumbing, and stone; they could write
080:72: About two thousand years later; 375 chosen people led by Sato
080:74: The Aegean region passed through five stages of culture, each less spiritual than the one before (80:7.6). On Crete the mother cult of Cain's descendants, which glorified Eve, spread widely; it lasted until the time of Christ and seeped into early Christianity in the form of the exaltation of Mary (80:7.7). By about 6500 B.C. the spiritual heritage of the Andites had greatly declined, and by about 5000 B.C. the three purest lines remained in Sumer, northern Europe, and Greece (80:7.8-7.9). Settlements also arose on Cyprus, near Carthage, and in Spain and Italy, and the Greeks, as gifted teachers and artists as well as traders and colonizers, left countless cultural outposts in the west (80:7.10-7.13).
080:76: The Andites mixed with the blue men to the north and, toward the western Mediterranean, with the mixed groups of Saharans and southern blue men. Between these two branches, broad-headed Andonite mountain tribes had long been settled (80:8.1). The book explains that the ancient Hittites came from the Andonite stock, and that this strain passed through Abraham's ancestors and contributed to the facial features of his descendants (80:8.2).
080:77: The Danubians were Andonite farmers and herders who moved north through the Balkans along the Danube valley, and their northernmost settlement was Liège in Belgium. The farther they went from the source of their culture, the faster they declined (80:8.4). Under the influence of Cretan missionaries they became mother worshipers, and they had the custom of cremating their dead inside stone huts (80:8.5).
080:79: The book explains that by the end of the Andite migrations the racial mixtures of Europe had settled into three white races (80:9.1). Through the Baltic amber trade and contact with the Danubians, the Nordics took up mother worship and cremation, which is why the remains of the early whites survive only as ashes (80:9.4). Around 2500 B.C. the westward push of the Andonites caused the most serious and lasting cultural setback up to that time and produced the Alpine race (80:9.6-9.7).
080:85: Blue man and Andite, with the blue heritage the largest
080:86: At first long-headed, tall, and blond
080:91: Andite and blue man, with secondary Sangik strains
080:92: The most mixed; short and long-headed
080:94: In this period mother worship flourished in Scandinavia and sun worship in southern France and Spain, and traces of these remain in megaliths such as Stonehenge and in the folklore of Brittany (80:9.13-9.14). But the book states plainly that insisting on this threefold classification is a fallacy. There has been so much blending that even the groups of 3000 B.C. were no more of one race than are the present inhabitants of North America (80:9.15). The book concludes that the future of North America depends on the quality of its population and the level of the social culture it maintains (80:9.16).

080:99: Paper 80 shows the long journey of the wave of culture that began in Eden as it flowed westward. Changes in nature—the Mediterranean turning into a sea, the Sahara becoming a desert, forests spreading across the Alps—altered the paths people took, and the coming of the horse gave the Andites swift movement. The book explains that in this process the union of the blue man and the Andites became the foundation of European civilization, but it does not hide the fact that the spiritual heritage grew steadily dimmer and that culture became less spiritual at each stage. And at the end it says that any attempt to divide the races into a few fixed branches is a fallacy. Peoples have already blended too deeply, and the book says the future depends on the quality of the population and the level of the culture a society maintains.

080:106: Drought in the Sahara and the flooding of the Mediterranean changed the paths of migration
080:108: The honest and artistic blue man became the biologic foundation of the European races
080:110: The horse gave the Andites swift movement and cohesion
080:112: The vigor of the blue man and the imagination of the Andites formed the northern whites
080:114: Egypt succeeded Mesopotamia as the center of civilization
080:116: Crete and Greece shone, but the spiritual heritage steadily declined
080:118: Broad-headed Andonites spread mother worship in central Europe
080:120: A threefold classification was once possible, but blending now makes it a fallacy
080:123: The culture that flowed out of Eden mixed with many peoples and became the foundation of Western civilization, but its spiritual heritage grew dimmer from generation to generation.
081:1: What power keeps the civilization evolution has built from collapsing and lifts it ever higher?
081:4: In Paper 80 we saw how the Andites spread westward and became the foundation of the civilizations of Europe, Egypt, and Greece. Now Paper 81 gathers up that long story of migration and sums up the tools, institutions, and conditions on which today's civilization stands.
081:5: The missions of Caligastia and Adam failed, yet the organic evolution of the human species did not stop; it kept carrying the races forward. Evolution can be delayed, but it cannot be stopped (81:0.1). The violet race was smaller than planned, yet the progress made since Adam has far surpassed the progress of almost a million years before him (81:0.2).
081:6: How, then, did mankind, once a race of hunters, become farmers, traders, and city dwellers? And what must the civilization we enjoy today safeguard if it is to keep on surviving?
081:8: ⟦Q 81:6.27⟧Intelligence may control the mechanism of civilization, wisdom may direct it, but spiritual idealism is the energy which really uplifts and advances human culture from one level of attainment to another.⟦/Q⟧ (81:6.27)
081:12: For about thirty-five thousand years after Adam, the cradle of civilization was southwestern Asia, stretching from the Nile valley through Mesopotamia to Turkestan. The decisive factor that settled civilization there was climate (81:1.1). When the changes in climate and land came to an end around 15,000 B.C., civilization came to a standstill worldwide, but the cultural ferment and biologic reserves of the Andites remained (81:1.2).
081:13: Now climate accomplished what all other efforts had failed to do: it made people give up hunting and turn to herding and farming (81:1.3). Because early farmers used many slaves, tilling the soil was long looked down upon, but in fact it is the greatest of all blessings (81:1.4). A diet combining wheat, rice, vegetables, and meat greatly improved the health and vigor of ancient mankind (81:1.8).
081:15: ⟦Q 81:1.3⟧Evolution may be slow, but it is terribly effective.⟦/Q⟧ (81:1.3)
081:18: The growth of culture depends on the development of the tools of civilization. Tools are useful only when they free human energy for higher tasks (81:2.1). Today we have a little leisure to think about society, but we must not forget that our early ancestors had almost no leisure to give to deep thought (81:2.2).
081:23: The first great discovery; in time it opened the door to science
081:25: Living tools — the way to agriculture and transport
081:27: An early institution that gave masters leisure
081:29: Ownership of land, which arose with agriculture
081:31: Primitive man did not see natural causes even in common phenomena like fire, and the story of Andon and the flint turned into the legend of Prometheus. But honest and fearless searching for true causes gave birth to modern science, turning astrology into astronomy, alchemy into chemistry, and magic into medicine (81:2.8-2.9). The Andites of Turkestan were the first to tame horses on a large scale (81:2.12), and scientific civilization is freeing man from endless toil by means of fire, wind, water, and electricity (81:2.14). Homes developed from caves to huts and then to brick houses, and the ideas of basketry and pottery arose by chance from mud huts (81:2.15-2.19).
081:33: From about 12,000 B.C., as climatic change ruined the grasslands of Turkestan, the superior Andites turned to trade and manufacturing (81:3.1). Trade brought different peoples into contact and speeded up the cross-fertilization of cultures (81:3.2), and about twelve thousand years ago the era of independent cities began. But the early cities were far from refined; with dust and refuse they rose a foot or two every twenty-five years (81:3.3).
081:34: Gold was the first metal people sought, and copper came into wide use once it was mixed with tin to make bronze. This bronze was produced by an Adamsonite of Turkestan who noticed a tin vein beside a copper mine (81:3.5). The Stone, Bronze, and Iron Ages existed side by side in different regions (81:3.4). The book says that traveling traders and explorers contributed more to historic civilization than all other influences combined (81:3.7).
081:39: Greater than all other influences combined
081:46: By the dawn of historic times, Eurasia, northern Africa, and the islands of the Pacific were covered with composite races in which the five basic stocks had mixed and mixed again (81:4.1). The book explains that the structure of the whole skeleton reveals origin better than the shape of the skull, and it says that there were originally five skeletal types (81:4.3).
081:61: Because these mixed so widely, the five types cannot be clearly distinguished in remains from the last twenty thousand years, and skeletal study shows mankind falling roughly into three classes (81:4.9-4.10). In many places, such as northern China, the Levant, India, and South America, these three classes are themselves mixed together (81:4.14).
081:66: Andite blend of Nodite and Adamic stocks
081:68: Primary Sangik — red, yellow, and blue
081:70: Secondary Sangik — orange, green, and indigo
081:73: Biologic evolution and cultural civilization do not always go together, but over the long course of history they are linked as cause and effect. Adam and Eve did not bring in strange new skills, but Adam's blood raised the brain power of the races and hastened economic and industrial progress (81:5.1). The book says that cultural society is not a privileged club in which everyone receives a free membership, but an association of those who work to leave a better world to their descendants (81:5.3).
081:74: Social union is a kind of survival insurance. People pay the premium of self-sacrifice and limits on their liberty, and in return they gain better group protection (81:5.4). Might does not make right, but every right is bound up with social obligations (81:5.6).
081:88: ⟦Q 81:5.7⟧Liberty subject to group regulation is the legitimate goal of social evolution.⟦/Q⟧ (81:5.7)
081:91: Waves of culture went out from the Euphrates valley many times, but they grew steadily weaker, and the pure Adamic strains were all scattered. There is now no source of culture and no Andites left to stimulate civilization anew, so the present civilization must be preserved and fostered (81:6.1). The book lists fifteen factors in which today's civilization is rooted (81:6.2).
081:96: Resources, climate, and terrain shape the character of a culture
081:98: Culture does not grow in poverty; leisure is essential
081:100: Knowledge is power; printing speeds up progress
081:102: A fitting population; wise is the people that knows when to stop
081:106: A common language widens peace and culture
081:108: Machines free human power for more valuable work
081:110: Home, play, and school pass culture on to the next generation
081:112: The ideals of one generation cut the channels for the next
081:114: The more specialization grows, the more co-ordination is needed
081:116: Ways of guiding people into suitable jobs
081:120: Co-operation in bearing burdens together depends on leadership
081:122: Experiment without fear, but without haste
081:124: The danger in moving from old ways to new
081:126: Among these factors the book especially stresses the power of ideals. No stream rises higher than its source, and the driving power of even the most material civilization lies in society's least material achievements (81:6.27). In the twentieth century travel and communication increased greatly, but education and ethical awareness have not grown to match, and modern civilization is standing still in spiritual development and in safeguarding the home (81:6.25). At first the struggle was for existence, now it is for a standard of living, and next it will be for quality of thinking (81:6.28).
081:127: A high civilization is born when material wealth, intellectual greatness, moral worth, social cleverness, and cosmic insight are wisely blended (81:6.38). The greatest danger is the breakdown that comes in passing from proven old ways to better but untried new ones, and civilization is not truly in peril until able leadership disappears (81:6.41-6.42). Since the invention of printing, human society has been rushing forward with the accumulated momentum of all the ages (81:6.44).
081:129: Paper 81 sums up at a glance the long struggle mankind has waged since Adam to build civilization. Climate turned hunters into farmers, and fire, domesticated animals, metals, cities, and trade gave people a little more leisure, bit by bit. Upon races mixed and mixed again, society became an insurance by which people protect one another, and liberty grew into the maturity of accepting group rules. But there is now no outside source to stimulate civilization anew. We must preserve and foster today's civilization ourselves, and the power that upholds that work to the end is not machines or wealth but the ideals carried on by homes, schools, and leaders—spiritual idealism.

081:136: Fire, animals, slaves, and private property gave mankind leisure
081:138: Trade and exploration were the greatest forces spreading civilization
081:140: The five original types have blended and now remain as roughly three classes
081:142: Society is insurance, and liberty that accepts regulation is the goal
081:144: Fifteen factors must be safeguarded, and their driving power is spiritual ideals
